entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4858"/><div sID="gen7112" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4858"/><hi type="bold">17. strange--</hi>His breath by elephantiasis had become so strongly altered and offensive, that his wife turned away as estranged from him (<reference osisRef="Job.19.13">Job 19:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.17.1">17:1</reference>).<div eID="gen7112" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7113" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">children's ... of mine own body--</hi>literally, "belly." But "loins" is what we should expect, not "belly" (womb), which applies to the woman. The "mine" forbids it being taken of his wife. Besides their children were dead. In <reference osisRef="Job.3.10">Job 3:10</reference> the same words "my womb" mean, my mother's womb: <hi type="bold">therefore translate, "and I must entreat (as a suppliant) the children of my mother's womb"; that is, my own brothers--</hi>a heightening of force, as compared with last clause of <reference osisRef="Job.19.16">Job 19:16</reference> [Umbreit]. Not only must I entreat suppliantly my servant, but my own brothers (<reference osisRef="Ps.69.8">Psa 69:8</reference>). Here too, he unconsciously foreshadows Jesus Christ (<reference osisRef="John.7.5">Joh 7:5</reference>). <div eID="gen7113" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 17. strange-- His breath by elephantiasis had become so strongly altered and offensive, that his wife turned away as estranged from him ( Job 19:13 ; 17:1 ). children's ... of mine own body-- literally, "belly." Not only must I entreat suppliantly my servant, but my own brothers ( Psa 69:8 ). Here too, he unconsciously foreshadows Jesus Christ ( Joh 7:5 ).

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4861"/><div sID="gen7117" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4861"/>20. Extreme meagerness. The bone seemed to stick in the skin, being seen through it, owing to the flesh drying up and falling away from the bone. The Margin, "as to my flesh," makes this sense clearer. The English Version, however, expresses the same: "And to my flesh," namely, which has fallen away from the bone, instead of firmly covering it.<div eID="gen7117" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7118" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">skin of my teeth--</hi>proverbial. I have escaped with bare life; I am whole only with the skin of my teeth; that is, my gums alone are whole, the rest of the skin of my body is broken with sores (<reference osisRef="Job.7.5">Job 7:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.102.5">Psa 102:5</reference>). Satan left Job his speech, in hope that he might therewith curse God. <div eID="gen7118" type="x-p"/>

That this truth is not further dwelt on by Job, or noticed by his friends, only shows that it was with him a bright passing glimpse of Old Testament hope, rather than the steady light of Gospel assurance; with us this passage has a definite clearness, which it had not in his mind (see on <reference osisRef="Job.21.30">Job 21:30</reference>). Tradition would inform him of the prediction. Foster shows that the fall by the serpent is represented perfectly on the temple of Osiris at Philæ; and the resurrection on the tomb of the Egyptian Mycerinus, dating four thousand years back. Job's sacrifices imply sense of sin and need of atonement. Satan was the injurer of Job's body; Jesus Christ his Vindicator, the Living One who giveth life (<reference osisRef="John.5.21">Joh 5:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.5.26">26</reference>).<div eID="gen7127" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7128" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">at the latter day--</hi>Rather, "the Last," the peculiar title of Jesus Christ, though Job may not have known the pregnancy of his own inspired words, and may have understood merely one that comes after (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.45">1Co 15:45</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.1.17">Re 1:17</reference>). Jesus Christ is the last. The day of Jesus Christ the last day (<reference osisRef="John.6.39">Joh 6:39</reference>).<div eID="gen7128" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7129" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stand--</hi>rather, "arise": as God is said to "raise up" the Messiah (<reference osisRef="Jer.23.5">Jr 23:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.18.15">De 18:15</reference>).<div eID="gen7129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7130" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">earth--</hi>rather, "dust": often associated with the body crumbling away in it (<reference osisRef="Job.7.21">Job 7:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.17.16">17:16</reference>); therefore appropriately here. Above that very dust wherewith was mingled man's decaying body shall man's Vindicator arise. "Arise above the dust," strikingly expresses that fact that Jesus Christ arose first Himself above the dust, and then is to raise His people above it (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.20">1Co 15:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.23">23</reference>). The Spirit intended in Job's words more than Job fully understood (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.12">1Pe 1:12</reference>). Though He seems, in forsaking me, to be as one dead, He now truly "liveth" in heaven; hereafter He shall appear also above the dust of earth. The Goel or vindicator of blood was the nearest kinsman of the slain. So Jesus Christ took our flesh, to be our kinsman. Man lost life by Satan the "murderer" (<reference osisRef="John.8.44">Joh 8:44</reference>), here Job's persecutor (<reference osisRef="Heb.2.14">He 2:14</reference>). Compare also as to redemption of the inheritance by the kinsman of the dead (<reference osisRef="Ruth.4.3-Ruth.4.5">Ru 4:3-5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.1.14">Ep 1:14</reference>). <div eID="gen7130" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4867"/><div sID="gen7131" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4867"/>26. Rather, though after my skin (is no more) this (body) is destroyed ("body" being omitted, because it was so wasted as not to deserve the name), yet from my flesh (from my renewed body, as the starting-point of vision, <reference osisRef="Song.2.9">So 2:9</reference>, "looking out from the windows") "shall I see God." Next clause [Job 19:27] proves bodily vision is meant, for it specifies "mine eyes" [Rosenmuller, 2d ed.]. The Hebrew opposes "in my flesh." The "skin" was the first destroyed by elephantiasis, then the "body." <div eID="gen7131" type="x-p"/>
